text: You already know what a table looks like from SQL: named columns, one row per record. In Python, the library that gives you that table is pandas. Everything in this chapter and the next one is built on two objects: the Series and the DataFrame. Learn these two well, and the rest of pandas reads like a natural extension of what you already know.

A Series is a one-dimensional column of values with a label attached to each one. If you followed the NumPy chapter, think of it as a NumPy array that carries an index and an optional name. Build one from a list of prices, giving it an index of A1, B2, C3, and the name price. Printed out, the left column is the index, the right column holds the values, and the footer shows the name and the data type.

Pull a value out by its label — prices at B2 gives you 45.0. Dot-mean gives the average, 25.83. And math applies to every value at once, exactly like the vectorized operations from NumPy — prices times 2 doubles every entry while keeping its label. The index is what makes a Series more than a plain array: labels travel with the values, so when you combine two Series later, pandas lines them up by label rather than by position.

A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table: several Series that share the same index. The most readable way to build one by hand is a dictionary where each key is a column name and each value is a list for that column. Here's a small customers table we'll reuse throughout the course — a customer id, a name, a city, and a segment for five customers. Compare this directly to a SELECT star from customers in SQL — the columns are the same idea. The row labels on the far left are new — that's the index, and since we didn't supply one, pandas created a default RangeIndex counting from 0.

Select one column with square brackets and you get a Series back — type of customers bracket city returns pandas dot core dot series dot Series. Printed, it shows the same five rows with the city name and its dtype, object. This is the key mental model: a DataFrame is a dictionary-like collection of Series that all share an index. Anything you can do to a Series, you can do to a column.

Four attributes answer the first questions you should ask about any table. Dot-shape gives you 5 comma 4 — rows, then columns. Dot-columns lists the column names. Dot-index shows the RangeIndex, start 0, stop 5. And dot-dtypes shows customer underscore id as int64, with the rest as object — that's how plain strings are stored in pandas 1.x, and it's one of the first things you check when a column doesn't behave the way you expect. Notice these are attributes, not method calls — no parentheses after any of them.

To recap: a Series is one labeled column of values, and a DataFrame is a table of Series sharing an index. Build one from a dictionary of lists, pull out a column with brackets to get a Series back, and use shape, columns, index, and dtypes to describe what you have. Next lesson, we stop typing data by hand and load a real file.
